title: From processing lines to dietary intake: a hierarchical Bayesian Monte Carlo framework for prioritizing technogenic microplastic exposure
content: Human dietary exposure to microplastics (MPs) presents a critical environmental health challenge, yet quantitative evaluation remains constrained by data sparseness, heteroscedasticity, and parameter uncertainty. This study developed an empirical hierarchical Bayesian regression framework integrated with Monte Carlo simulation (10 000 iterations) to quantify probabilistic exposure across food matrices. Utilizing the FOMIC-Py dataset, the model incorporated logarithmic transformation [ln(MPs + 1), ln(consumption + 1)], empirical Bayes shrinkage, and category-specific partial pooling to evaluate four consumption scenarios. Diagnostic evaluations confirmed that logarithmic transformation resolved heteroscedasticity (Breusch–Pagan p = 0.55) and residual non-normality (Shapiro–Wilk p = 0.74), outperforming 31 candidates of statistical, kinetic, and machine learning models (log-scale R2 = 0.825). Estimated mean annual exposure was 27.2 mg (95% uncertainty interval: 12.3–52.5) for standard consumers (15 kg per year) and 71.3 mg (27.8–152.9) for extreme consumers (50 kg per year), with exceedance probabilities above 50 mg per year at 3.3% and 72.9%, respectively. Technogenic pathways dominated exposure, led by dairy (23.3%), grains (19.2%), and beverages (11.3%), driven by processing wear, thermal stress, and high-torque capping rather than trophic bioaccumulation. Superlinear response patterns (elasticity >1) were identified in beverages and oils, whereas vegetables exhibited strong baseline contamination with sublinear scaling. This framework provides a statistically robust architecture for uncertainty propagation, risk prioritization, and science-based regulatory mitigation strategies.
